messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet Nguyen was sixty years old, a fisherman who had worked the Gulf waters out of Biloxi, Mississippi, since he was a teenager. He was married to Linh, his wife of thirty-eight years, and they had raised three children together. The traumatic event had happened eighteen months ago, on a calm October morning. Kiet and his younger brother, Bao, had been hauling in a net when a sudden squall capsized their skiff. Kiet managed to grab a floating cooler and was rescued within hours, but Bao’s body was never found. For weeks afterward, Kiet had searched the shoreline himself, walking the mudflats at dawn, certain he would find his brother alive. He never did.

In the months that followed, Kiet began to change in ways that puzzled and frightened him. The first thing he noticed was the physical reactivity: whenever he stepped onto the dock and smelled diesel fuel and brine, his chest would tighten, his hands would shake, and a wave of nausea would roll through him. He had come to believe that these bodily sensations meant he was losing control, that something terrible was about to happen again. This belief—that his own body was a warning system he could not ignore—had grown directly out of a deeper conviction he could not shake: that people could not be trusted. He had trusted Bao to watch the weather that morning, and Bao was gone. Kiet now believed that relying on anyone was a mistake, that the only person he could count on was himself, and even that felt uncertain. This mistrust colored everything. When his son offered to help repair the engine on the boat, Kiet refused, insisting he would do it alone, even though his hands ached from arthritis. He had become certain that if he let anyone close, he would be responsible for losing them too.

The physical reactions, in turn, fed back into his bleak view of the world. Each time his heart pounded and his breath grew shallow on the water, Kiet would think, *See? This is proof. You cannot trust yourself. You cannot trust anyone. You are still in danger.* The loop tightened: the more his body reacted, the more he felt that the world was unsafe, and the more unsafe he felt, the more his body reacted. He began to avoid the boat entirely, telling his wife he was taking a break, but the real reason was that he could not bear the feeling of his own terror. He stayed home, sitting in the dark living room, watching television with the sound off. The emotional numbness crept in slowly. He noticed that when his granddaughter hugged him, he felt nothing—just a hollow pressure against his chest. He had begun to say to himself, *I feel dead inside,* and the phrase no longer felt like an exaggeration; it felt like a fact.

The survival guilt was a quieter, more persistent presence. It surfaced in the middle of the night, when sleep would not come. Kiet would lie awake, replaying the moment the skiff tipped, wondering why he had grabbed the cooler and not his brother. He had come to believe that he should have died instead, that Bao had been the better man—kinder, more patient, with a young wife and a baby on the way. These thoughts did not cause his physical reactivity directly, but they lived alongside it, a separate, heavy weight he carried into every sleepless hour. The sleep problems themselves had become a nightly ritual: he would fall asleep for an hour, then jolt awake with his heart racing, certain he was back in the water. The anger came in flashes—at the weather, at the boat, at himself—and then disappeared, leaving only the deadness behind.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a moment on the dock three weeks ago. His son had asked him to come out for a short run, just to test the new engine. Kiet had walked to the edge of the pier, looked at the water, and felt his legs give way. He sat down on the wooden planks, unable to stand, unable to speak, while his son watched in confusion and then in fear. That night, Linh told him quietly that she could not keep watching him disappear. Kiet agreed to see a counselor, though what frightened him most was not the therapy itself—it was the possibility that after all this time, he might still have to get back on that boat.
